newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa hikes key Bank rate one point to 17 pct.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa hikes key Bank rate one point to 17 pct.

text.p: South Africa's central Reserve Bank said on Wednesday it was increasing its key Bank rate to 17 percent from 16 percent, effective from November 21.
Governor Chris Stals said in a statement the move was necessary given the instability of the rand, rising short-term money market rates and the threat of higher inflation.

"The unstable conditions in the market for foreign exchange, recent developments in the domestic financial markets and the growing upward pressures on inflation all dictate a need for tightening monetary policy at this stage," Stals said.

"The Reserve Bak has therefore decided to follow recent interest rate trends in the financial markets and raise the Bank rate, that is the rate at which the Bank is prepared to make loans to banking institutions on an overnight basis, from 16 to 17 percent as from tomorrow."

Stals said the high money market shortage, which averaged more than nine billion rand a day in the first 20 days of this month, had forced up short-term interest rates, with call money now standing at 17.00 percent from 15.50 at end-September.

"The level of the Reserve Bank's rate for loans to banking institutions at 16 percent has now fallen out of line with other interest rates and the banks are increasingly relying on this source of relatively cheap funds for balancing their cash requirements."
In these circumstances the Bank had two options -- to increase liquidity by injecting more money into the system, or to raise the Bank rate.

Injecting extra cash would increase already unacceptably high rates of money supply growth and fuel inflation. Consumer price inflation is already running at an annual rate of 9.1 percent in October, the highest level since June 1995, according to figures released earlier on Wednesday, Stals noted.

"Taking account of the expected further pressures emanating from the depreciation of the rand, it will be a suicidal approach for the Reserve Bank to create even more central bank money in this situation," Stals said.
The fall in the currency, totalling 22.2 percent on a trade-weighted basis so far this year, was clearly overdone, he added.

The further depreciation of about five percentage points in October, in particular, no longer reflected basic economic developments such as the rand's purchasing power parity, the global competitiveness of the South African economy or cyclical trends in the current account.
"The further depreciation of the rand in October represented a step in the wrong direction that now begs for action," he said.
